body_markdown:
It wasn’t possible for me to talk about the cheapest new car available to the American consumer in 2026, the Hyundai Venue, and not be reminded of the cheapest car from 40 years ago, when I was still pretty green at automotive journalism. (That was a time, which is perhaps of no interest to anyone else, when you kind of needed a degree in journalism to badge yourself a “journalist,” instead of just an iPhone.)


Already, I’m digressing. The cheapest car in 1986 was the[$3995 Yugo](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/40-years-ago-we-met-the-yugo-and-it-was-rough-whats-with-the-redux/) , imported, of course, from Yugoslavia, by my old friend Malcolm Bricklin. By necessity—largely because I *do* actually have a degree in journalism—I am and always have been poor, but when listening to Bricklin, I sat up, back arched, head cocked to one side like the old RCA dog, hanging on his every word: If I had any money to invest, it would probably have been in one of Bricklin’s adventures, be it bicycles with electric motors—decades ahead of their time—his reboot of the Fiat 124 spyder, his Bricklin SV sports car, or the Yugo. He was an *incredible* salesman.


Flickr/Alden Jewell


That Yugo beat, by a thousand bucks or so, the debut that same year of the Hyundai Excel. Like the Yugo, it was loosely based on a dated Fiat design. It’s faint praise to point out that the Excel was a substantially better car than the Yugo, though that’s scarcely an endorsement. If you see either one on America’s roads today, it’s because the car is an ironic novelty item, not because it has served the driver so well over four decades that he or she just can’t part with it.


Until the Yugo showed up, my only exposure, before or since, to Yugoslavia’s automotive industry was when my wife’s Toyota Tercel badly needed new tires and, per usual, I was broke. I went to Discount Tire, and they sold me a set of Tigars, which were nice and wide and oddly heavy and looked really good on the little yellow Toyota. Maybe a year later, I was driving the Tercel home from work when (aside from racing incidents), I suffered the only blowout of my life, when the left rear Tigar just exploded. Fortunately, cars came with actual spare tires then.


Wisely, I had bought the warranty from Discount, and when I returned, the manager told me that, perhaps for obvious reasons, they no longer stocked the Yugoslavia-made Tigar. He offered me a set of tires from a company I had actually heard of for, I think, 20 bucks. Sold! One reason I still do business with Discount Tire.


## Specs: 2026 Hyundai Venue SEL


**Base Price:** $24,250/$24,645 as tested
**Powertrain:** Inline 1.6-liter four-cylinder, Continuously Variable Transmission
**Output:** 121 hp/113 lb-ft of torque
**Layout:** front-engine, front-wheel drive, four-door, five-seat SUV
**Weight:** 2612 pounds
**EPA-rated Fuel Economy:** 29 mpg city/33 highway/29 combined
**Competitors:** Chevrolet Trax, Nissan Sentra, Kia K4


So when it came time to spend a week in a Yugo, I thought it was my duty. I had to pick it up from a dealer, a day later than agreed upon because they wanted to make “some adjustments” to the bright-red Yugo they’d received from the distributor. I was less than a block away when I became aware of at least a half-dozen things that didn’t work, some of them important, such as the turn signals. The takeaway from this: The dealer spent *an entire extra day* fixing problems? I wonder what *else* didn’t work when it arrived?


My daily commute to the newspaper, located in downtown Dallas, was about an 85 mile-round trip. I left my car at the dealership and headed home in the Yugo. It did not have air conditioning, so that was one thing, at least, that was not broken. Only a subsequent test of a Suzuki Samurai rivaled the Yugo for outright terror on Interstate 45, with the two sharing some traits that included lane-wandering, a jarring ride, uncomfortable seats, and a powertrain that allowed me to pass not one single vehicle, except in both cases, a garbage truck.


As I did with the Samurai, I phoned my contact and said I won’t be needing this car for the entire week. Those are the only two times I’ve asked to give a vehicle back early.


Now I wish I had a Samurai. Don’t wish I had a Yugo, although the convertible was kind of scarce and interesting.


2027 model shown.


Hyundai


Which brings us to 2026’s cheapest car, although when we talk about the Hyundai Venue, the manufacturer-preferred term of “most affordable” works better than “cheapest.” Not only because I have been a (rather quiet) fan of the Venue since it debuted as a 2020 model, priced just north of $17,000, but because Hyundai has consistently made small but perceptible improvements to the car as the price has gradually climbed.


The 2026 Hyundai Venue SE, the, er, *least expensive* of the three models, has an advertised starting price of $20,550, with a total sticker, minus dealer-installed options, of $22,700. That includes what is shown on the sticker as “Inland freight and handling.” Evidently Hyundai is willing to ship it from Korea to the U.S. by boat for free, but is billing upwards of $1600 to ship it to your town. Even given diesel prices, that’s a pretty healthy number.


Hyundai


Hyundai


Hyundai


Hyundai


Using Hyundai’s online vehicle search, I found one Venue SE up the road with a sticker price of $22,460, apparently delivered prior to today’s fuel prices. Compared to the other two models—the monotone SEL, and the two-tone SEL—the SE is amazingly well-equipped, as a lot of stuff on it is there either because the federal government requires it or because it would cost Hyundai more to remove. This includes the four-wheel disc brakes, Android Auto and Apple CarPlay, the six-speaker sound system, and the tilt-and-telescoping steering wheel.


Hyundai


And safety-wise, you still get electronic stability control and traction control, a bunch of airbags, forward collision avoidance assist, lane-keeping assist, a rearview camera, rear-seat alert, and “Driver Attention Warning.” Anyone who’s of voting age or beyond should know that it wasn’t so long ago when that safety equipment would cost you thousands extra. And yes, you *do* need it.


The Venue SEL’s 17-inch wheels


Hyundai


What you don’t get in the SE is 17-inch alloy wheels (15-inchers are standard), wireless charging, heated front seats and side mirrors, keyless entry, a power sunroof, a leather-wrapped steering wheel, and a few other admittedly nice features. The SEL models we found ranged from $24,500 to a little over $25,000.


As it often is now between the least and most expensive models, the powertrain is the same, in this case a reasonably well-behaved 1.6-liter four-cylinder with 121 horsepower, mated to a continuously variable automatic transmission, as building a CVT is apparently cheaper—there, I used *that* word—than a transmission with gears. While the 2020 Venue was offered with a manual transmission, the new one is not. EPA-rated fuel mileage is 29 mpg city, 33 highway, and 29 overall, regardless of the 15- or 17-inch wheels and tires.


Hyundai


My test car was a two-tone Venue, a kind-of gray that Hyundai calls “Denim,” with a white roof, which I think gives the car a moderately premium appearance. The cloth interior was also Denim. The front seats were surprisingly accommodating even for a day trip; I’m six feet tall, and with the driver’s seat set for my height, I can ride quite comfortably in the rear. Luggage space (Hyundai says the Venue is an SUV, by the way) is 18.7 cubic feet with the rear seat up, or 31.9 with it down.


Instruments and controls are particularly well-designed, both for aesthetics and ease of operation. As it was with the original six years ago, there are three driving modes: Normal, Sport, and Snow. “Sport” really isn’t; I kept it in “Normal.” The simple suspension—MacPherson struts and coil springs up front, torsion bar in the rear—works fine, aided by satisfactorily grippy Korean-sourced Nexen 205/55-R17 radials that worked well in the rain.


Places that you might expect Hyundai to cut corners—leave off a rear window wiper, for instance—are handled by higher-quality features than you might expect.


All that said, where you buy your Hyundai Venue matters. A dealer in my area has a Venue with a list price of $25,100. It had “Added Features” that totaled $625 in dealer-installed equipment, from a $45 first aid kit to $240 for carpeted floor mats. There is little there you couldn’t get at Walmart much cheaper. But that dealer’s website also says you’ll need a $1298 “Pre-Delivery Service,” a “Private Tag Agency Fee of $189,” and an “Electronic Registration Filing Fee of $595.” I’m not saying that $2082 is a lot to charge for that, but you be the judge. It may not be a dealbreaker on the purchase of a $65,000 Hyundai Palisade, but if you’re buying a Venue, there’s a good chance that two thousand bucks is a lot of money. With that, the sermon concludes.


I like the Venue, and I would be pretty happy to have one as a daily driver, or delighted to send a child off to college in one. Yes, it’s “the cheapest” new car available, but it’s such a far cry from that 1986 Yugo that I can almost—almost, but not quite—forget what it was like getting passed by a half-dozen nose-to-tail 18-wheelers on the way home.


Hyundai


## 2026 Hyundai Venue SEL


**Highs:** Price, surprisingly comfortable, roomier front and rear than you’d expect.


**Lows:** Sport setting isn’t sporty, fuel mileage isn’t stellar, and neither is the power.


**Takeaway:** As the entry-level, cheapest new car in America, the Venue SE is unexpectedly competent and easy on the eyes.
